notes.meaning: Jehoshaphat became king of Judah after his father Asa died. He immediately took steps to protect his northern border against the kingdom of Israel, where King Ahab was ruling. He did not seek an ungodly foreign treaty like his father had done, but prepared wise defenses so his people would be safe.

Jehoshaphat placed military forces in all the walled cities throughout Judah. He also stationed military posts in the towns of Ephraim that his father Asa had taken from the northern kingdom. These troops guarded the people and kept the nation's borders secure against sudden attack.

The Lord helped and guided Jehoshaphat because the king followed the faithful example of King David's early years. David had served God wholeheartedly before his serious sins involving Bathsheba and Uriah. Jehoshaphat also refused to worship the Baals, which were the false idol gods of the surrounding nations.

Jehoshaphat prayed only to the true God of his ancestors and obeyed His commands. He refused to copy the sinful practices of the northern kingdom of Israel, which worshiped God through golden calf statues. He chose to follow God's law rather than the bad examples around him.

God made Jehoshaphat's rule strong and secure because of his obedience. The people of Judah brought him voluntary gifts out of deep love and respect for their king. Because God blessed his faithful leadership, Jehoshaphat enjoyed great wealth and honor.

Jehoshaphat took great courage and joy in serving the Lord, rather than becoming proud of his wealth. He removed the pagan shrines and the wooden poles used to worship the false goddess Asherah. He wanted his entire country to be free from idol worship.

Early in his reign, Jehoshaphat sent five royal officials, nine Levites, and two priests throughout the towns of Judah to teach. The royal officials used the king's authority to gather the people and back up the teachers. The priests and Levites were the ministers whose special job was to explain God's law clearly to everyone.

This teaching team traveled throughout all the cities of Judah carrying the written Word of God. They used the Scriptures as their textbook so the people could learn what God required of them. Teaching God's truth helped bring unity, obedience, and peace to the entire nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this nationwide teaching tour as an idealized story created after the exile, reflecting later Jewish devotion to the law rather than an actual historical event under Jehoshaphat.

notes.meaning: God placed a holy fear into the hearts of the kingdoms surrounding Judah so they would not attack. When those nations saw Judah turning to God and flourishing under His blessing, they did not dare to start a war. True spiritual revival gave the country greater safety than any army could provide.

Neighboring nations respected Jehoshaphat so much that they brought him tribute to keep peace. Some Philistines brought large gifts of silver, and Arab tribes brought thousands of male sheep and goats from their flocks. These gifts showed that even foreign peoples recognized how God was blessing the king.

Jehoshaphat grew steadily stronger and more influential. He built fortresses to guard the country and store cities to hold food and military supplies. He used his time of peace wisely to make the nation secure against future trouble.

The king kept large stores of supplies in the towns throughout Judah. In the capital city of Jerusalem, he also stationed elite soldiers who were brave and ready for battle. His careful planning kept the nation prepared for any threat.

The fighting men of Judah were organized under three main commanders, totaling 780,000 soldiers. Adnah served as the head commander, followed by Jehohanan and Amasiah. Amasiah was specially remembered because he willingly dedicated himself to serve the Lord and his people.

The tribe of Benjamin provided two divisions totaling 380,000 men. Eliada commanded troops who were skilled with bows and shields, while Jehozabad led soldiers equipped with regular battle weapons. Together with the men of Judah, they formed a well-organized defense force ready to protect the land.

These trained divisions were at the king's direct service, in addition to the garrisons stationed in walled cities across Judah. Most of these men lived on their own land during peacetime but were ready to serve whenever the king called. Even with such great forces, Judah's real strength remained in the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see the army total of 1,160,000 men as unrealistically large for such a small region, suggesting the numbers were either damaged in copying or exaggerated to emphasize God's blessing.
